groups.title: Money: dues, the ledger, and the books

cards.title: From a notice to a fee to a lien
cards.why: A published schedule and a guaranteed hearing are what make enforcement accepted by the people it touches. Owners stay in the loop on their own property.

qs: Should the resident be guaranteed a hearing before a lien?
rows.rec: A homeowner can ask for a hearing at every stage, up to and including the escalation to a lien. A lien is never recorded while a hearing request is open.
rows.reply:
Has counsel reviewed any state's rules for HOAhx yet? We recommend that the launch automate none: each community enters its own notice, cure, hearing and lien deadlines from its documents, and any community without them is flagged for manual review. The rest of your answer we will build as you wrote it.

Everything else we will build as you wrote it.

qs: Should tenants be able to appeal violations, given the owner is ultimately liable?
rows.rec: A tenant who is the subject of a notice can respond to it and dispute it, with photos, and the owner is told of every notice and every response on their property.
rows.reply:
we recommend a change. One community setting: who may file an appeal, owner only (the default) or owner or tenant. The tenant can always respond with evidence; the owner is copied on every notice, response, deadline and decision; everything is logged. The rest of their answer as written.

Everything else we will build as you wrote it.

cards.title: Votes, elections, and meetings
cards.why: A single ballot meeting quorum is the kind of default that embarrasses a board later. Not certifying your own election is basic fairness.

qs: What is the quorum default, and who sets it?
rows.rec: Every formal vote requires a quorum entered as a percentage of entitled properties, taken from the community's rules when the vote is created. There is no default of one, and a vote that closes short of quorum is recorded as failed for want of a quorum.
rows.reply:
Proxy voting: can it come after launch? We recommend yes. At launch each vote shows that proxies are not counted in HOAhx, and everything else you asked for quorum is built.

Everything else we will build as you wrote it.

qs: Are meetings complete enough: agendas and minutes exist, but no notices, RSVPs, or attendance?
rows.rec: Meetings ship as they are: agenda, location, and minutes, plus the board roster, role dates, and decision records. Meeting notices, RSVPs, and attendance tracking are not in the launch.
rows.reply:
Meetings: at launch HOAhx would carry agendas, attachments, approved minutes, the decision record, and the notice sent with its delivery record. Can attendance, quorum status and motions follow after launch? We recommend yes.

Everything else we will build as you wrote it.

cards.title: The community feed and events
cards.why: Approval before posting kills a community feed. Comment moderation with a reason is enough for the rare problem.

qs: Should the community feed be moderated before or after posting?
rows.rec: The feed stays moderated after posting: a post or a comment can be hidden or removed with a reason. Nothing waits for approval before it appears.
rows.reply:
The community feed: at launch it would carry post-moderation, and moderators hiding or removing a post or a comment with a reason kept in the history. Can reporting a post, the rules shown on the feed, spam filters, automatic holds, appeals and approval for member events follow after launch? We recommend yes.

Everything else we will build as you wrote it.

qs: Who can post to the community feed, and can posting rights be withdrawn from an individual?
rows.rec: Board and management roles post; residents comment and react. Taking one person's commenting rights away for a set period comes after launch, if a community needs it.
rows.reply:
Residents starting their own posts is a change from the launch plan. We recommend it at launch, together with a moderator's restriction of one person (a reason, a notice to them, an end date), where the person answers the notice to appeal. Is that all right?

Everything else we will build as you wrote it.

cards.title: Architectural reviews
cards.why: For a homeowner with a contractor waiting, the deadline on the application is the answer to "what happens next".

qs: Should architectural decisions have a required response time?
rows.rec: Each application type the community sets up carries a decision deadline, thirty days by default, shown to the homeowner and the reviewers. An application past its deadline appears as overdue on the board dashboard. Nothing is approved automatically.
rows.reply:
we recommend a change. When a community's documents say an application is approved once the deadline passes, HOAhx tells the board and the homeowner that the deadline passed, and the board records the approval. Nothing is ever approved automatically. Everything else as they wrote it.

Everything else we will build as you wrote it.

cards.title: Messages and announcements
cards.why: Officers covering for each other need to read the thread; the fix is to say so on the screen. A policy pasted into an announcement belongs in the library anyway.

qs: Should managers, the President, and the Secretary be able to read every conversation in the community?
rows.rec: Managers, the President, and the Secretary can read every conversation with the office, as now, and the message screen says so plainly, so nobody mistakes a thread with the office for a private one.
rows.reply:
Messages to the office: at launch each community chooses which roles read them, the resident sees exactly who can read before sending, and every access is recorded. Can restricting sensitive conversations to designated people follow after launch? We recommend yes.

Everything else we will build as you wrote it.

cards.title: HOAhx Copilot: the provider and its monthly cost
cards.why: At launch scale the cost is tens of dollars a month, and the cap keeps it there. Your decision is the cap, not the vendor.

qs: Which provider should power HOAhx Copilot, at what monthly cost, and should it be in the launch or follow it?
rows.rec: Copilot ships in the launch, as on your Core list. Jacob selects and connects the provider, a hosted language-model service billed per question (about two cents a question), on an account in HOAhx's name, with a monthly cap of $50 and a warning at $35. You approve the cap and the card it goes on; the provider can be swapped later without changing what homeowners see.

cards.title: Two people claiming the same home
cards.why: Rare, but today the bill goes to whoever was recorded first. A checked record is the only fair tie-breaker.

qs: Who is authoritative when a property has two people claiming ownership?
rows.rec: When two people claim ownership, an administrator verifies the deed or the closing record before the primary-owner designation changes. One primary owner per property is enforced, and the outcome is recorded with its evidence. Until it is verified, the owner on record stays primary and the bills keep going to them.

cards.title: Pricing: the three loose ends
cards.note: Your plans, prices, tiers and trial terms are recorded. These three points were left open in your requirements document.
cards.why: Each of these has an answer that is simple to say at checkout. A founding rate rewards the communities that take the first step without a discount that never ends.

qs: On an annual plan, what happens when the number of homes changes mid-term?
rows.rec: On an annual plan the home count is checked at renewal only: no mid-term charge when homes are added, no mid-term refund when they leave. The new tier applies from the renewal and is shown at checkout.
rows.reply: Thank you. We agree: no mid-term charge or refund within the paid tier, the home count is checked at renewal, and the renewal price is shown in advance. We will add your point: if a community grows beyond its tier's maximum, the administrator is notified and must approve before the plan changes or anything more is billed.

cards.title: Who may appoint an HOA Administrator
cards.why: The HOA Administrator runs a community day to day. Letting the management company appoint one means a managed community does not wait on a board meeting to be staffed.

qs: May a Property Manager or a Management Company Administrator appoint an HOA Administrator?
rows.rec: The President, a Property Manager, or a Management Company Administrator can appoint an HOA Administrator. An HOA Administrator cannot appoint another one. If you want the board alone to hold that appointment, the two management roles lose that one permission and nothing else changes.

cards.title: A board-only document sent for signature
cards.why: A rule with one exception hidden in the download path is a rule that will be misread, and nothing the communities do today needs it.

qs: May the office send a board-only document to a homeowner for signature, so that homeowner can open that one document to sign it?
rows.rec: No: a document a homeowner is asked to sign is one they may read, so the office publishes it to residents before asking for a signature, and a request to sign a board-only document is refused. If the exception should stay, it becomes the rule: a homeowner asked to sign a board-only document may read that version, before and after declining.

cards.title: A community always keeps a President
cards.why: The President is the only community role that appoints and removes board roles, so a community without one can appoint nobody and stays stuck until someone outside it acts. Closing one's own account is a right the app stores require of every app.

qs: Must a community always have a President, so that nobody in the community can remove, deactivate or archive its only one?
rows.rec: Keep it: a community keeps a President. The role is handed on before its holder is removed, and HOAhx can step in when a President is gone. If the rule should hold HOAhx staff too, it is one condition and one test.

qs: Should the only President of a community be asked to hand the role to someone else before they close their own account?
rows.rec: Leave it for the launch: the right to close one's own account stands, and HOAhx appoints the next President when it happens. A hand-over step on the account-closing screen ("give the President role to someone first") is a candidate for after the launch.

cards.title: When a homeowner's membership ends, the home goes with it
cards.why: "Removed" should mean removed: a person the board has ended should not keep reading the home's codes, ledger and household through a record the board cannot see.

qs: When the board deactivates, archives, or marks a homeowner as moved out, should that person lose access to their home in the app as well as to the community?
rows.rec: Keep it: ending a person's membership ends their access to the community and to the home, the records stay, and restoring the account brings the access back. If an owner who has moved out should keep signing in to a home they rent out, the office keeps their membership active and records the move-out on the tenant instead.

cards.title: When a homeowner pays twice
cards.why: An alert should mean someone probably made a mistake, not that someone paid early. A credit someone asked to have back should not be spent by AutoPay while the treasurer decides, and a request nobody answers should not lock it away for good.

qs: A homeowner with a credit asks for the money back. Until the treasurer decides, should AutoPay leave that credit alone, and for how long? And how often may a homeowner ask?
rows.rec: Keep thirty days and one request a month: once a homeowner asks for a credit back, AutoPay leaves it alone until the treasurer decides or thirty days pass. Add two buttons before launch: the treasurer can decline with a short note to the homeowner, and the homeowner can change their mind and keep the credit.
rows.reply: Thank you. We will reserve only the requested amount while a request is open, so AutoPay can still apply any remaining credit; the request goes to the treasurer, a second authorized approver issues any refund, and the homeowner can withdraw it and keep the credit. We will add a reminder to the treasurer when a request is still open after five business days. One open request per account at a time works for us, and we recommend keeping the thirty-day limit as an outer bound rather than releasing the credit sooner. If you would rather have no time limit, tell us and we will keep the credit reserved until the treasurer decides.

cards.title: Opening balances brought in from your spreadsheet
cards.why: A balance belongs to the home, not to a person; the figure should be the same for every owner and should not look overdue before the community starts.

qs: When a home has more than one owner, whose account does the opening balance from your spreadsheet go on?
rows.rec: The first active owner of the home; the balance stays on the home's ledger, so every owner of the home sees the same figure.
rows.reply: Thank you. The balance goes on the home's ledger, so every owner of the home sees the same figure, and it is attached to the first active owner. We will add your safeguards: a preview with the homes matched, the credits and amounts owed and totals that can be checked against your spreadsheet, a block on importing the same file twice, the import date and source in the account history, and an authorized administrator's confirmation before any balance affects resident notices, AutoPay or collections.

qs: What date should an opening balance from your spreadsheet carry on a home's ledger?
rows.rec: The approval day, so nothing looks overdue before anyone could see it.
rows.reply: Thank you. We recommend the approval day as the date the balance carries on the ledger, so nothing looks overdue before anyone could see it, and we will keep your cutover date and any original due dates and aging from the spreadsheet on the record. A balance that arrives as one total is marked as imported and held for administrator review before any overdue notice, fee or collection. If you would rather the ledger carry the cutover date, tell us and we will do that, with the same hold on notices and fees until the administrator approves.

cards.title: Amending a published budget
cards.why: Preparing figures is already their job, and nothing reaches residents without the board's recorded approval.

qs: Who may start an amendment to a budget the board has already published?
rows.rec: Keep it as built: whoever may prepare the budget may start an amendment; only the President records the board's approval and publishes it.

qs: When an amended budget is published, who should be told, and how?
rows.rec: Keep it as built: one in-app notice each to the board and to residents, no e-mail.

qs: What should residents see of the board's approval of a published budget?
rows.rec: Keep the minutes on the board's screen; residents read the minutes in Documents when the board shares them there.

qs: Which documents may the board attach as the record of a budget approval?
rows.rec: Keep it: the approval is backed by the meeting minutes, and the board files the minutes first.

cards.title: Plan changes and pricing for larger communities
cards.why: Nothing has been paid, so there is nothing to make up or refund; a charge inside a free trial is the opposite of what the trial promises.

qs: When a community changes its HOAhx plan during the free trial, what happens?
rows.rec: The new plan starts at once and nothing is charged during the trial. The trial keeps its end date, and the first charge at its end is the new plan's price.

qs: When a community moves to a different plan that costs the same, when does it take effect?
rows.rec: On the next billing date, nothing charged or refunded now, told as "a plan change at the same price".

qs: How should the price work for a community with more than 500 homes? Today the five flat tiers run to 458 homes, then every home pays the same monthly per-home rate from 459 homes, with no upper limit.
rows.rec: Keep the per-home rate from 459 to 500 homes. A community above 500 homes does not buy in the app: the screen says HOAhx sets up its plan with it, and HOAhx sets that community's price and setup fee.

cards.title: Tenants and rental managers for a home
cards.why: This was the earlier recommendation, and it keeps the owner, who knows the lease, in charge of the tenant's access.

qs: May a homeowner invite their own tenant and choose what the tenant may use and until when?
rows.rec: Yes, as built.

qs: An owner who rents out a home can name a rental manager (a rental company or a person) for that home, with a start and end date. What may the rental manager do?
rows.rec: Pay the home's dues with their own payment method, receive the home's notices and send maintenance requests for it; never vote, never see the owner's saved payment details or other homes. The owner, or the board at the owner's request, names and removes them, and every change is in the home's history.

cards.title: Architectural request types and parking permits
cards.why: The days to decide are the board's commitment to homeowners, so the person who decides should set them; adding the Administrator later is a small change.

qs: Who sets up a community's architectural request types: the kinds of request, what each must include, and the days to decide?
rows.rec: Keep it with the President, the person who decides architectural requests, for launch; let the HOA Administrator do it too only if a community asks.

qs: Which documents should a household keep on a vehicle before the community gives it an active parking permit?
rows.rec: Keep it as built.

qs: When a household changes the license plate on a vehicle that has an active parking permit, what should happen to the permit?
rows.rec: Keep it as built.

cards.title: Account-status letters, the card fee and refund requests
cards.why: A lender or a title company usually acts within a month; a shorter window keeps an old balance from being read as current, and a homeowner can create a new letter at any time.

qs: For how long should a lender or a buyer be able to check a homeowner's account-status letter online?
rows.rec: Keep it as built: 30 days.

qs: Should the account-status letter say plainly that it is not a resale or estoppel certificate?
rows.rec: Keep it as built.

qs: Who may create an account-status letter for a home?
rows.rec: Keep it as built.

qs: When a card payment that carried the convenience fee is refunded, should the fee be returned too?
rows.rec: Keep it as built.

qs: Should AutoPay by card add the convenience fee to each automatic payment?
rows.rec: Keep it as built: no fee on AutoPay at launch.

qs: After the treasurer declines a refund request, may the homeowner ask again in the same month?
rows.rec: Keep it as built.

qs: Who may answer a homeowner's refund request (refund it, decline it, or keep the credit)?
rows.rec: Keep it as built.

qs: Which communities count as founding communities, and what do they keep?
answered.rec: Founding communities: the first ten communities that subscribe by January 31, 2027 keep their monthly price for twenty-four months, whatever the list price does. Nothing else is discounted.
answered.build: Owners' "HOAhx Trial, Billing & Onboarding Requirements" (Google Doc, Sep 9, read Sep 10) plus the Sep 9 pricing sheet. Tiers (boundary confirmed by Jacob 2026-09-28, recorded 2026-10-01 so Tenyson and Jake build to one structure): $59 (1–50 homes, $1.18 a home at 50), $89 (51–100, $0.89 at 100), $129 (101–200, $0.65 at 200), $179 (201–300, $0.60 at 300), $229 (301–458, down to about $0.50), then from 459 homes $0.50 per active home per month on every home, no further tiers. 459 is the crossover because $229 ÷ $0.50 = 458 homes, so 459 homes = $229.50 and the two halves meet without a step. This replaces the doc's 301–500 and the sheet's "through 449". All MVP features included; no Basic/Pro/Premium packages. Trial: 30 days, no card, full product on the community's real data, guided setup from day one; expires to a locked read-only state; data kept 90 days; reactivation by purchasing; advance notice before deletion. Monthly conversion: normal monthly rate + a one-time "Community Implementation & Launch" fee, charged through the subscription's payment method; first paid month at 100% by default; HOAhx staff may apply a one-time 50% discount to the first paid month (manual, once, does not change the standard price). Annual: no recurring discount; first year = 11.5 × monthly (50% off the first month equivalent) with the implementation fee waived, collected as one payment; renewals at 12 × the then-current monthly rate, shown clearly at checkout. Implementation fee: $49 (1–50), $99 (51–100), $149 (101–200), $199 (201–300), $249 (301–500), $299 starting point above 500, configurable. Home count: active property/unit records in HOAhx at each billing date (occupied or vacant; future phases don't count); tier changes apply from the next charge, never retroactively, in both directions; notify the administrator before a new amount is charged; annual terms keep counting and should support a prorated adjustment on a material increase (the doc's own note: "clarify"). Card fee: "no idea until NMI" — pending the NMI agreement. Founding rate: not addressed in either document — still open. The doc also specifies a trial lifecycle beyond the plan catalogue: welcome on day 1 with internal capture of start/expiry/homes/admin; a day 7–10 activation check with an internal alert on low activity; day 14 and day 21 board-approval questions (capturing the next board-meeting date, flagging high-intent or needs-follow-up); a day 28 reminder by status; internal-only trial extensions (7 days, 14 days, custom date) with original/new dates, grantor, and reason recorded and no extension the community can request for itself; twelve internal sales statuses; and an internal activity timeline of trial and conversion events. That lifecycle is outside SB2 and the twelve items — see `changes.md` Proposed 2026-09-10.

answered.rec: The subscription price is the price: HOAhx absorbs the card cost on a community's own subscription, and an annual plan can also be paid by bank transfer.

qs: When a homeowner pays more than they owe, when should the treasurer be alerted?
answered.rec: Keep it as built: the treasurer and the president are alerted when a homeowner pays twice in one dues period or pays more than was owed, once per home per period. No alert for a homeowner who simply pays ahead, or who pays in two parts.
answered.build: Keep it as built, with the owners' additions: alert the treasurer and the president when a homeowner pays twice in one dues period or pays more than was owed, and flag likely duplicate payments or unexplained account credits for the treasurer to review; apply legitimate payments to the right current or future charges; keep excess money as a credit by default and tell the homeowner; a refund needs a second authorized approver; log the payment, credit, review and any refund in the account history.

qs: If a tenant pays the dues for a home, may the tenant ask for a refund of a credit on that home's account, or only the owner?
answered.rec: A tenant may ask for a refund only when the owner has let them see the balance and pay. The money always goes back to the card or account it came from, and the owner is told when a tenant asks.
answered.build: Yes, as recommended, with the owners' conditions: a tenant may ask only for a credit traceable to the tenant's own payment and only when the owner has allowed the tenant to pay; the owner is told when the request is submitted; it goes through the normal approval with a second approver; a refund goes only to the original payment method; the tenant sees the full account balance only if the owner separately allows it.

answered.card: Telling a new resident the board's answer
qs: Should HOAhx email a person when the board approves, declines, or asks for more proof on their request to join?
answered.rec: Yes: one short email for each answer: approved, declined with the board's reason, or more proof needed. The waiting screen says an email will follow, so nobody has to keep checking the app.
answered.build: Yes: email the person and notify them in the app when the board approves, declines or asks for more proof. For more proof, say what is missing and how to send it; for an approval or a decline, give the outcome and next steps without private board discussion. The waiting screen says they will be notified, so nobody has to keep checking.

answered.card: Opening balances brought in from your spreadsheet
qs: If a homeowner starts with a credit from your spreadsheet, may AutoPay use it before the community's start date?
answered.rec: Keep and show the credit; AutoPay waits for the start date.
answered.build: Agreed: keep the imported credit and show it as pending until the community's start date; do not lose it or reduce it before then.

answered.card: Changing a plan's price for communities already paying
qs: When HOAhx changes the price of a plan after communities are already paying on it, what happens to those communities?
answered.rec: Communities already paying keep their price until HOAhx moves them, with at least 30 days' notice before any new price is charged. It matches the rule for home-count changes and avoids a surprise bill.
answered.build: Agreed: communities already paying keep their price until HOAhx moves them, with at least 30 days' written notice before any new price is charged. A monthly plan takes the new price no earlier than the next billing date after the notice; an annual plan keeps its price through the paid term and changes at renewal, with advance notice. The first ten communities that subscribe by January 31, 2027 keep their starting monthly price for 24 months.

qs: Who pays the card processing cost: the homeowner as a convenience fee, or the community?
answered.rec: A homeowner who pays by card pays the card cost, shown as its own convenience-fee line before they confirm. A bank payment costs nothing. Where NMI says a card fee is not allowed in a community's state, that community absorbs the cost and the screen says so.
answered.build: The homeowner pays the card cost as a convenience fee, shown as its own line with the total before they confirm. Bank payments stay free. To your question about where a card fee is not allowed: card network rules do not allow a fee on some cards (debit cards, for example), and a few states limit or ban card fees. NMI confirms in writing which cards and states that covers before any fee is switched on. On those cards and in those states no fee is charged, the community covers the card cost, and the screen shows no fee line.

answered.card: Late fees, and an autopay charge that fails
qs: What should happen when an autopay charge fails: retries, notice, escalation?
answered.rec: When an autopay charge fails, the homeowner is told the same day with the reason and a one-tap retry. HOAhx retries once, three days later. After a second failure autopay pauses, the homeowner and the treasurer are told, and the balance stays due until the homeowner pays or fixes the payment method.
answered.build: Agreed: two retries (3 and 7 days after the first failure), only for failures the processor marks retryable, none after a hard decline or a stop-payment; retries stop once the home is paid or AutoPay is off; and late fees follow the grace period, never the failed attempt. The sandbox test results are met by the payment verification and will be sent before this is marked complete.

answered.card: Setting up the community's merchant account
qs: Should a management company be able to run its communities' payments through its own existing merchant account?
answered.rec: NMI Payments only. No bring-your-own-processor for the launch. The first management company that asks starts a conversation, not a build.
answered.build: Only HOAhx's own gateway is accepted. Each community has its own merchant account that settles to its own bank, and there is no bring-your-own-processor mode; that stays an option for after launch. The boarding part of the sandbox test waits on the processor's pricing and boarding; the rest is covered by the payment verification.

qs: Should reconciliation be required before a month or year can be closed?
answered.rec: Closing a month is offered and recommended, not required. The close screen shows how many entries are still unmatched to a deposit, and a report from an unclosed month says so at the top. A required close is a later step if the first treasurers ask for it.
answered.build: What we settled when we talked it through.

answered.card: What a homeowner sees of the money
qs: Should residents see the community's full ledger, or only their own?
answered.rec: A homeowner sees their own property ledger, the published budget, and budget versus actual spending. The community's line-by-line ledger stays with the board.
answered.build: The plan already. Homeowners see their own ledger, the approved budget, budget against actual, and published statements; the community's detailed ledger stays with the board and finance. Records owners are entitled to are shared through the document library, where each document's audience is set.

qs: Should the budget require board-vote approval rather than one President click?
answered.rec: The President publishes the budget alone, and the board's vote is minuted in the meeting's decision record. A required recorded vote inside the publish step stays on the candidate list for after launch.
answered.build: The President's click no longer counts as approval. The budget goes Draft, Approved, Published; approval records the approving board or committee, the date, the vote outcome and the minutes or resolution, and it cannot be published without them.

qs: Should a published budget be amendable mid-year?
answered.rec: A mid-year change is published as a replacement budget for the same year, linked to the one it replaced, so both stay visible with the date and the reason.
answered.build: An amendment is published as a new version for the same year, linked to the original, which stays unchanged, with the reason, effective date, approval and publish date; the board and residents are told.

qs: Should the platform produce a reserve-study report, and is the delinquency report enough for what boards must file?
answered.rec: The delinquency report, with its aging buckets and export, ships. No reserve-study report for the launch; it stays on the candidate list.
answered.build: Built the way you asked, in your words above.

qs: Is month-by-month auditor access the right scoping model?
answered.rec: An auditor's access is granted from a screen by the President or the Treasurer: the months, the document types, and an end date. Month by month stays the model; an annual audit is granted as twelve months.
answered.build: Built the way you asked, in your words above.

qs: How long do Auditor and Attorney scopes last, and who sets them?
answered.rec: An attorney's access is granted per matter by the President or the Secretary, with an end date the community chooses (one year by default) and can renew. Both lapse on their date, and the board can see who has access and until when.
answered.build: Built the way you asked, in your words above.

answered.card: From a notice to a fee to a lien
qs: Should there be a mandatory waiting period between a notice and a fee?
Should fee amounts be constrained by a published schedule?
answered.rec: Every violation category carries a published schedule: the fee amount and the time the homeowner has to respond, set by the community (14 days by default). No fee before that time passes, and no fee outside the schedule.
answered.build: Built the way you asked, in your words above.

answered.card: From a notice to a fee to a lien
qs: Should escalation to a lien require a recorded board vote rather than one President action?
answered.rec: The President approves an escalation to a lien alone, with a required written reason, and never on their own property. A required board vote inside the step stays on the candidate list.
answered.build: The community records its collections policy and who approves a routine escalation; disputed charges, large balances, exceptions and foreclosure need a second approval; conflicts step aside; each escalation keeps its reason, balance, notices, documents, approver and time, and the kind of step (lien, recorded notice, referral, foreclosure).

qs: Are there response-time commitments per priority?
answered.rec: No fixed response time per priority. Every request gets a deadline when staff triage it, shown to the homeowner, and "urgent" puts the request at the top of the queue. The form's promise that urgent requests are escalated immediately comes off until an escalation exists.
answered.build: Built the way you asked, in your words above.

qs: Should residents be able to close their own tickets when satisfied?
answered.rec: Staff or the assigned vendor mark a request resolved. The homeowner then confirms the fix, or reopens the request with a reason within fourteen days of that resolution; after that they send a new request. A homeowner cannot close a request staff have not resolved, and can withdraw their own request at any time.
answered.build: Staff or the vendor mark the work complete, the resident has 7 days (the community can change it) to confirm or reopen, a reminder goes before it closes as "Closed, no response", and the resident can reopen it later. A resident cancels before dispatch, or asks staff to cancel after.

qs: Should vendors see the resident's name, unit, and contact details?
answered.rec: An assigned vendor sees the request, its photos, the resident's name and unit, and the resident's replies, and never the email, the phone, staff notes, or costs.
answered.build: Agreed, with the refinement. The assigned vendor sees only that work order: the unit, the issue, relevant photos, access instructions and the messages needed for the repair; staff notes, estimates, costs and unrelated resident information stay private. Contact is through in-app messaging or a masked method by default; an authorized HOA user may share a specific detail, and the time it was shared is recorded. Vendor access ends when the work order closes or the assignment is removed.

qs: Is 90 days the right maximum vendor assignment window?
answered.rec: A vendor's assignment lasts up to ninety days. Staff and the vendor are reminded a week before it lapses, and staff renew it with one tap.
answered.build: Most is built (access tied to one work order, 30 days by default, a reminder before it lapses, staff extend it). I add a required reason on each extension. A long project is extended again with a new date, up to 90 days at a time.

qs: Should two spots per property be a community setting rather than a platform constant?
answered.rec: The number of spaces each property starts with is a community setting in the parking rules, two by default. Staff can still add spaces to one property by hand.
answered.build: The number of spaces is a community setting (two by default), with rules by home type if needed; a staff exception needs a reason and is recorded; the community's total is enforced; resident parking stays separate from guest passes.

qs: Who validates a pass in practice, and how?
answered.rec: A pass is checked by whoever the board designates: a board member, an administrator, or the towing contractor, by entering or scanning the pass code on their phone. No gate hardware and no separate gate-staff role for the launch.
answered.build: The plan already. Board, management and a designated towing company check a pass by code or scan on a phone, see only what they need, each check is logged, and towing stays the community's own process.

qs: Is President-only certification correct, and what happens if the President is a candidate?
answered.rec: An authorized officer certifies and publishes a vote result. A candidate never certifies their own election: if the President stood, the Secretary, or another officer who did not stand, certifies.
answered.build: The community names who may certify; a candidate or anyone with a conflict cannot; if the President is a candidate another officer or an assigned inspector certifies; results publish only after certification; ballots stay secret.

qs: Should event RSVPs support guests, or only members?
answered.rec: An event RSVP carries a guest count that counts toward capacity, and board members can RSVP too.
answered.build: An RSVP carries guests who count toward capacity, the community sets a guest limit per event, remaining capacity is shown, and board members RSVP like everyone else.

qs: Is President-only architectural decision correct?
answered.rec: The community assigns reviewers per application and names who decides, with the President as the default. Nobody reviews or decides an application on their own home.
answered.build: Each community names its architectural committee or reviewers and who decides; the President only where the community chooses; conflicts step aside; assignments, recusals and decisions are recorded.

qs: Is the native acknowledgement workflow legally sufficient for the documents being signed?
answered.rec: HOAhx's own electronic signature ships: the signer's identity, intent, and time, the exact version signed, a signed copy, and the evidence history. Whether that is enough for a given document is for the community's counsel; an outside signature service can be added after launch if a community needs one.
answered.build: Built the way you asked, in your words above.

qs: Which documents must every resident sign, and what happens if they refuse?
answered.rec: The community marks which documents are required, and every household is asked to sign them at onboarding. A refusal is recorded with its reason and shown to the board as an open item. Nothing is enforced automatically.
answered.build: The community marks required documents and who signs each one (owner, tenant, each adult); an acknowledgment is kept apart from an agreement; a refusal is recorded with its reason as an open item with reminders; nothing is enforced automatically.

qs: Who may see the community's governing documents: residents only, or prospective buyers too?
answered.rec: Documents stay members-only. A prospective buyer receives the governing documents inside the transfer package the seller requests, not through an account.
answered.build: What we settled when we talked it through.

qs: Should document versions ever be deletable, for example on legal advice?
answered.rec: A document version is never deleted. On legal advice, the board takes a document down: it is hidden from everyone but the board, with the reason recorded, and its files, signatures and history are kept. Bringing a taken-down document back is not offered at launch. The administrator's document actions are repaired so each one works or says why not.
answered.build: Much is built (no version can be deleted in the app; take-down with a reason; legal holds). I add limiting a confidential or legal-advice document to named people and counsel, and permanent deletion only after the retention period, with no hold, by an authorized administrator with approval.

answered.card: What reaches the phone, and what cannot be switched off
qs: Are there communications a resident may not opt out of: emergency notices, legal notices, dues reminders?
answered.rec: Legal and enforcement notices, dues and payment notices, and urgent community alerts cannot be switched off. An urgent alert still reaches each person only on the channels they keep on (the app, email or text), so it never forces a channel they turned off. Announcements, request updates, and community messages can be switched off, channel by channel.
answered.build: They agree with my recommendation. Emergencies, legal and enforcement notices, dues and payment notices, and account security cannot be switched off and stay in the in-app history; optional messages can be. A push alone never counts as formal delivery of a legal notice.

answered.card: What reaches the phone, and what cannot be switched off
qs: Which notifications should reach the phone by default: announcements, request updates, payment reminders?
answered.rec: On the phone, announcements, request updates, and payment reminders are all on by default. Quiet hours hold the non-urgent ones overnight, and each person can switch any of the three off.
answered.build: Build as written with the phone apps: payment reminders and own-request updates on by default once allowed, routine announcements off, safety alerts separate, quiet hours, everything kept in the app, permission asked in context, nothing private on the lock screen.

answered.card: What reaches the phone, and what cannot be switched off
qs: Should text-message notifications be connected for the launch, or should the launch ship with push and email only?
answered.rec: Push notifications and email ship with the apps. Text messages are built for the launch as an option each community switches on: each person's consent is recorded, a reply of STOP is honored, quiet hours are respected except for urgent alerts, and the cost per message is shown to the community before it turns them on. If you would rather launch without them, they stay switched off.
answered.build: The launch carries notices in the app, by push and by email. Text messages come after launch, optional for each community and each person, with their own consent. Text messages and their provider setup leave the launch.

qs: Is a 10,000-character announcement limit right?
answered.rec: The announcement limit of 10,000 characters stays. Anything longer is attached from the document library.
answered.build: Keep the 10,000-character limit, show a counter and a clear message, link longer notices to library documents everyone receiving it may open, and show a short preview in email and push.

answered.card: What is kept, for how long, and what a resident can take with them
qs: What is the data retention policy, per record type?
answered.rec: Financial records, seven years. Violation and enforcement records, seven years after the violation is closed. Visitor logs, one year. Messages and announcements, three years. Audit records, for the life of the community. Personal data is removed when an account is deleted. These periods go into the app-store privacy disclosures, and each kind of record is deleted automatically when its period ends, unless a legal hold stops it. Which violations count as closed (cured, passed reinspection, lien satisfied) is for the community's counsel to settle; until then those are kept.
answered.build: Built the way you asked, in your words above.

answered.card: What is kept, for how long, and what a resident can take with them
qs: What is the retention period for messages and announcements?
answered.rec: Messages and announcements follow that policy: three years, no separate rule.
answered.build: Built the way you asked, in your words above.

answered.card: What is kept, for how long, and what a resident can take with them
qs: How long is visitor access history retained, and who may see it?
answered.rec: Officers and managers see the whole visitor log; each resident sees their own entries. The log is kept for one year.
answered.build: Residents see their own home's visitors; the full log only for staff each community authorizes, with each view recorded; the one-year deletion becomes a community setting.

answered.card: What is kept, for how long, and what a resident can take with them
qs: Is there a data export or deletion path for a resident who requests one?
answered.rec: A resident deletes their account and personal data in the app; their community records (requests, payments, notices) stay with the community. An export of their data is requested from HOAhx support and delivered within thirty days; a self-serve export comes after launch.
answered.build: Closing an account is separate from export and deletion; for launch a support-assisted request (identity checked, tracked, an export of only that person's data, official records referred to the community); 30 days is our own target, not a legal deadline; self-service export after launch.

answered.card: Who gets the alerts, and the monthly spending alert
qs: Who receives the error, uptime, and spending alerts, and what is the monthly spending cap?
answered.rec: The same two people receive the error, uptime, and spending alerts. The hosting account is set to alert at $150 a month, with an earlier warning at $75. That is a notice, not a spending cap: Google Cloud cannot stop the bill at a number, it can only tell you the number was passed. The accounts run comfortably under both today, and a lower number would page you for nothing.
answered.build: Alerts to Dan and Rustin at three monthly spending thresholds with a forecast alert, covering every production project, tested with both before October 9; it is a notice, not a cap.

answered.card: Who gets the alerts, and the monthly spending alert
qs: Who is notified when a security rule denies an unexpected access, and is anyone watching?
answered.rec: Unexpected access denials are counted and reach the same people as a daily summary; a sudden spike alerts within minutes.
answered.build: Immediate alerts on denials involving money, standing in for a user, administrator access or another community's data, to Dan, then Rustin, and Jake; user, action, community, time and a reference, nothing sensitive; who acknowledges is written down and the flow tested before October 9.

qs: Should a balance adjustment stay capped at what the home owes?
answered.rec: An adjustment can bring a home's balance down to zero and no further. It can clear a debt, but it can never turn one into money the community owes the homeowner. When money genuinely has to go back to a homeowner, that is a refund, which already needs two financial people.
answered.build: Accepted: an adjustment stops at zero, overpayments stay a credit, refunds need two approvers and each adjustment is recorded. One more check at approval in case the balance changed.

answered.card: Gate and guest codes for tenants
qs: Should an active tenant see the home's gate and guest codes?
answered.rec: A tenant living in the home sees its gate and guest codes, the same as the owner, and loses them the day the tenancy ends. Another household never sees them. If you would rather the codes stay with the owner alone, a tenant is shown who to ask instead.
answered.build: Yes. An active tenant sees their home's gate and guest codes and never another home's. Community staff change the codes at launch; an owner or tenant asks for a change in HOAhx. When a tenancy ends the person's access is removed, the owner and staff are prompted to review and change the codes (a code the tenant already knows keeps working until it is changed), and codes are kept out of notices and exports.

answered.card: How far back a restore can reach
qs: Should a daily backup be kept for 30 days and then deleted?
answered.rec: A copy of every community's records is taken each night and kept for 30 days, then deleted automatically. Anything that went wrong in the last month, such as a bad import or a deletion nobody noticed, can be put back. A longer window costs a little more storage and is a one-line change.
answered.build: Agreed. A daily backup is kept 30 days and then deleted automatically. Backups are encrypted, access is restricted, they hold all required community data and documents, and they are kept separate from the retention policy for financial records and other documents. The restore process is documented and a restore is tested before launch.

answered.card: Who reads a homeowner's written appeal
qs: When a homeowner appeals a violation in writing, should the Secretary and Treasurer read the appeal text as well as the people who decide it?
answered.rec: Keep it: whoever may read the case reads the homeowner's appeal, and only the roles who may review a violation decide it. If the appeal should be narrower, the read narrows to the roles who decide, and the Secretary and Treasurer see that an appeal exists without its text.
answered.build: Change. Give the full appeal text only to the assigned case administrator and the people authorized to decide that specific appeal under the community's governing documents and applicable law; not to the Secretary or Treasurer by default (they see that an appeal exists, its status and its deadlines unless assigned to the case). Access is case-specific, an authorized administrator assigns or removes reviewers, and who viewed or changed the appeal is logged.

answered.card: Co-owners seeing each other's requests and reviews
qs: Should the owners of one home see each other's maintenance requests and architectural reviews?
answered.rec: Yes: the owners of a home see each other's requests and reviews, on the request pages first and then on the home's timeline, so every row a co-owner reads opens. If not, each owner keeps seeing only their own.
answered.build: What we settled when we talked it through.

answered.card: Every tenant gets a tenant record
qs: Should every tenant have a tenant record, so the owner's switches apply to every tenant and not only to those the owner or the office added through the tenant forms?
answered.rec: Yes: every tenant gets a tenant record, created when staff assign the tenant role, with the switches off until the owner grants them, so every tenant is held to the owner's choices. If not, a tenant without a record keeps the access of a household member.
answered.build: Agreed. Every authorized tenant gets an individual tenant record tied to the correct home, however they were added (a tenant form, the owner, staff or an approved import), never a shared household login. The home's tenant access settings apply to every active tenant, each person's access stays individually manageable, who added or changed a tenant and when is recorded, and ending one tenancy ends only that person's access.

qs: Billing contacts, and handing over the account
answered.build: Built with the changes you asked for, in your words above.

qs: Cancelling, and taking the records along
answered.build: Built with the changes you asked for, in your words above.

answered.build: Built with the changes you asked for, in your words above.

answered.build: Built with the changes you asked for, in your words above.

answered.build: Built with the changes you asked for, in your words above.

answered.card: Falling behind, payment plans, the ledger and statements
qs: Statements, exports, and matching deposits
answered.build: Built with the changes you asked for, in your words above.

qs: Should partial payments be accepted against a dues balance?
answered.rec: Any amount from one dollar up is accepted. A payment above what is owed, including a second payment made by mistake, stays on the account as a credit, and AutoPay uses that credit first. A late fee still applies to whatever is left when the grace period ends.
answered.build: Any amount from one dollar up is accepted. A payment above what is owed stays on the account as a credit, AutoPay uses that credit first, and the homeowner can ask for it back. A late fee still applies to whatever is left when the grace period ends.

qs: Should tenants be able to pay dues by default?
answered.rec: A tenant can pay dues unless the owner switches it off on the tenant's record. The switch is repaired so it saves, and the owner is told whenever a tenant pays.
answered.build: Tenant payments are off by default. The owner switches payment on for a named tenant of that home and can switch it off again at any time. A tenant's payment posts to that home's ledger, shows the tenant as the payer, and the owner is told each time. Permission to pay gives the tenant nothing else: no wider view of the account, and the assessment stays the owner's responsibility. Switching it off also ends any AutoPay that tenant set up.

answered.card: Late fees, and an autopay charge that fails
qs: Are late fees ever calculated and applied automatically?
answered.rec: Late fees are applied automatically the day after the grace period on the community's dues schedule, at the amount on the schedule, and the homeowner is told the day it happens. A payment counts on the day it is submitted, not the day the bank settles it, so a bank payment started on time is never late.
answered.build: Late fees are applied automatically the day after the grace period on the community's dues schedule, at the amount on the schedule, and the homeowner is told the day it happens. A payment counts on the day it is submitted, not the day the bank settles it, so a bank payment started on time is never late.

answered.card: A returned bank payment, or a dispute
qs: Who should be told when a payment is disputed or a bank payment is returned?
answered.rec: The treasurer and the homeowner are told the same day, in the app and by email (and on the phone once the apps are out). The President sees it in the weekly board summary. The homeowner's notice says what was reversed, the deadline, and how to pay again.
answered.build: The homeowner and the Treasurer are told the same day, in the app and by email, and by text message only if the homeowner opted in. The Treasurer is the community's finance contact; where no Treasurer is seated, the President is. The notice says which of the two happened, in different words for each: a bank payment returned, or a card payment disputed. The homeowner's notice says what happened, what it did to their balance, and how to pay again. A dispute also opens an urgent task for the Treasurer with the processor's deadline and the next steps; the President is alerted to a dispute as the backup, without the card or bank details. Other board members see only that an item is open.

answered.card: A returned bank payment, or a dispute
qs: Should a returned bank payment carry a fee, and how much?
answered.rec: A returned bank payment carries a fixed fee the community sets in its payment rules, $25 by default, charged once per return and never above the state's cap. It appears on the homeowner's ledger with the reason.
answered.build: No returned-payment fee by default. A community may switch one on and set the amount in its payment rules after confirming that its governing documents and its state allow it. The fee is shown on the bank payment screen and in the AutoPay consent before the homeowner authorizes anything. It applies once per returned payment, only when the bank's reason is insufficient or uncollected funds, never to a card dispute, and it is never counted when a late fee is worked out. The setting stays unavailable to communities until NMI confirms in writing that the fee is allowed and where the return reason is reported.

answered.card: Setting up the community's merchant account
qs: Which roles may set up the community's merchant account?
answered.rec: The President or the Treasurer applies and signs. In a community with a management company, the property manager may start the application, but the President or the Treasurer signs it.
answered.build: The community's Account Owner, the President or the Treasurer opens the merchant application from HOAhx and submits it on NMI's page. For the launch, a property manager cannot open it. HOAhx records who opened the application, when, and every status NMI sends back. A management company starting an application on a community's behalf, with the board's recorded authorization and an officer still submitting it, is agreed as the rule and built when the first managed community is boarded.

answered.card: Setting up the community's merchant account
qs: Should the merchant application open on NMI's own page, or sit inside HOAhx's payment setup screen?
answered.rec: The application opens on NMI's own page from HOAhx's payment setup. The version embedded inside HOAhx is a later improvement, once NMI confirms it works on the partner sandbox and inside the phone apps.
answered.build: The application opens on NMI's own hosted page, started from HOAhx's payment setup. HOAhx collects and stores no bank, tax or identity details. When NMI answers, the community's payment setup shows one of four statuses in plain words (pending, more information needed, approved, declined) with what happens next and who has to act. The embedded version stays a later improvement.

qs: Should treasurers get logins to NMI's own merchant portal, or only the reports inside HOAhx?
answered.rec: Treasurers work inside HOAhx: deposit summaries, deposit history, and NMI's transaction reports appear there, and no separate NMI portal login is issued. If a particular treasurer needs one, HOAhx support asks NMI case by case.
answered.build: Treasurers work inside HOAhx for payments, refunds, returns and disputes, with filters and an export. No shared NMI login is ever issued. Bank deposits and NMI's processing fees are read in NMI's portal until NMI makes that data available to HOAhx, so each treasurer who needs it gets their own named NMI login, limited to viewing, with two-factor sign-in. Deposit and fee reports move inside HOAhx when NMI confirms the data.

answered.card: What a homeowner sees of the money
qs: Should residents be able to see their full payment history including refunds and disputes?
answered.rec: A homeowner sees their whole payment history, including refunds, returned payments, and payments under review for a dispute, each with its status, the reason, and what to do next. Internal notes and processor identifiers never appear.
answered.build: Yes. A homeowner sees their own whole payment history: the date, the amount, the payment method shown only by its type and last four digits, the current status, and any refund, returned payment or dispute, each with a plain explanation and the next step. Internal notes and processor identifiers never appear.

answered.card: Who gets the alerts, and the monthly spending alert
qs: Who is the named recipient of production alerts, and who is the backup?
answered.rec: Dan is the named recipient of production alerts, by email and text, with Rustin as the backup, and a one-page "when this fires" note: what to check, when to call Jacob, how to pause payments. Jacob is copied through launch and the thirty days after. Say so if it should be the other way round.
answered.build: Dan is the named recipient of production alerts, by email and text, with Rustin as the backup, and a one-page "when this fires" note: what to check, when to call Jacob, how to pause payments. Jacob is copied through launch and the thirty days after. Say so if it should be the other way round.

qs: Should Platform Support be able to see resident names and addresses at all?
answered.rec: Support sees a first name, a last initial, a masked email, and which communities and roles a person holds; never an address, a phone number, or a full name. A full household comes into view only through temporary support access that the community authorizes, with a reason, a scope, a time limit, and a complete record of what was done.
answered.build: Platform Support should see a resident's first name, last initial, masked email, community, and role by default. Full names, addresses, and phone numbers should be hidden. If a specific support issue requires more information, an authorized community contact must approve temporary, read-only access to only what's needed. That access must expire automatically and be fully logged. Support must never see full payment or bank details, impersonate a resident to take action, change resident or financial records, or perform financial actions. By authorized community contact, we mean the Community Account Owner, the designated Backup Owner, or someone the owner has explicitly granted Support Access Approver permission. Board members, residents, and Billing Admins should not have approval authority by default. The answer page and the demo's permissions should reflect this.

qs: Should a credit or an adjustment always need a second financial approver, with charges and fees left to one person?
answered.rec: One financial person can post a charge or a fee. A credit or an adjustment, anything that takes money off what a home owes, needs a second financial person to approve it, and nobody approves an entry on their own home.
answered.build: Please require a second financial approver for manual credits, write-offs, and adjustments that reduce a homeowner’s balance. The requester cannot approve their own entry, and no one can approve an adjustment to their own home. Exclude automatic credits tied to actual overpayments, and allow one authorized person to post routine charges or fees that follow the board-approved schedule. Log all entries and approvals with the amount, reason, user, and timestamp.

qs: Is the black HX tile the icon for both app stores and the phone home screen?
answered.rec: The designer's black HX tile is the icon in the App Store, on Google Play, and on the phone's home screen, with the 512-pixel version as the Google Play listing icon.
answered.build: The designer's black HX tile is the icon in the App Store, on Google Play, and on the phone's home screen, with the 512-pixel version as the Google Play listing icon.
